questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following physical quantities is dimensionless?

solution.explanation: Strain is the ratio of a change in a dimension (length or volume) to the original value of that dimension. A ratio of two like quantities has no dimensions.
solution.why_others_wrong: Stress has the dimensions of pressure, angular velocity has dimensions [T⁻¹] (the angle itself is dimensionless, the time is not), and impulse has the dimensions of momentum.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', dimensions of physical quantities

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Three lengths measured with different instruments are 12.5 cm, 3.27 cm and 0.418 cm. Their sum, written to the correct number of significant figures, is:

solution.explanation: In addition or subtraction, the result is rounded to the least number of decimal places among the numbers added. 12.5 cm has only one decimal place, so the sum is rounded to one decimal place.
steps: Least number of decimal places = 1 (in 12.5 cm)
solution.why_others_wrong: 16.188 cm keeps all the digits and claims more precision than the measurements have. 16.19 cm uses two decimal places, which only 3.27 cm has. 16 cm rounds to whole centimetres and throws away the reliable first decimal place.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', significant figures (rules for arithmetic operations)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The length and breadth of a rectangular sheet are measured as (5.0 ± 0.1) cm and (2.0 ± 0.1) cm. Its area, with the maximum absolute error, is:

solution.explanation: For a product Z = AB, the maximum relative error is the sum of the relative errors: ΔZ/Z = ΔA/A + ΔB/B. The absolute error is the relative error multiplied by the value of Z.
solution.why_others_wrong: ± 0.2 cm² adds the absolute errors directly, which is the rule for a sum, not a product. ± 0.07 cm² quotes the relative error as if it were the absolute error. ± 0.01 cm² multiplies the two absolute errors.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', combination of errors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (physical quantity) with List-II (a quantity having the same dimensions).

List-I:
A. Pressure
B. Gravitational potential (work done per unit mass)
C. Angular velocity
D. Surface tension

List-II:
I. Square of speed
II. Spring constant (force per unit extension)
III. Energy per unit volume
IV. Frequency

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Reduce each quantity to M, L, T. Pressure and energy per unit volume are both [M L⁻¹ T⁻²]; work per unit mass is [L² T⁻²], the same as speed squared; angular velocity and frequency are both [T⁻¹]; surface tension (force per length) and spring constant (force per extension) are both [M T⁻²].
steps: Pressure = N/m² = J/m³ → [M L⁻¹ T⁻²] → III
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes pair angular velocity with speed squared or surface tension with energy per volume; neither pair matches in M, L, T.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', dimensional formulae and dimensional equations
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The initial and final temperatures of a liquid are measured as (60.0 ± 0.5) °C and (40.0 ± 0.5) °C. The maximum percentage error in the fall in temperature is:

solution.explanation: For Z = A − B the maximum absolute error is ΔA + ΔB. Because the difference is much smaller than either reading, its percentage error is much larger than theirs; this is why subtracting nearly equal quantities is avoided in precise work.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.5% takes only one reading's error (0.5/20). 2.1% adds the relative errors of the two readings, which is the rule for a product. 0% assumes the two errors cancel, but the maximum error is found by adding them.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', combination of errors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Repeating a measurement many times with the same instrument and taking the arithmetic mean reduces the systematic error in the result.
Statement II: If the radius of a sphere is measured with a relative error of 1%, the maximum relative error in its calculated volume is 3%.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Random and systematic errors; error in a power
solution.explanation: Averaging many readings reduces random errors, which are equally likely to be positive or negative. A systematic error (a zero error, a wrongly calibrated scale) shifts every reading the same way, so the mean carries it unchanged; it must be removed by correcting the instrument or method. For V ∝ r³, ΔV/V = 3Δr/r.
steps: Statement I: averaging reduces random errors, not systematic errors → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is the trap: repetition cannot remove an error that has the same sign in every reading.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', errors in measurement
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The position of a particle moving along the x-axis is x = 3t² − 12t + 5, where x is in metres and t in seconds. Its velocity at t = 3 s is:

solution.explanation: Instantaneous velocity is the time derivative of position. Differentiate x(t) and substitute t = 3 s.
solution.why_others_wrong: −4 m/s is the position x(3) in metres, not a velocity. −3 m/s is the average velocity over the first 3 s, (x(3) − x(0))/3 = (−4 − 5)/3. 18 m/s keeps only the 6t term and drops −12.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', instantaneous velocity and speed

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two forces of magnitudes 3 N and 5 N act at a point, the angle between them being 60°. The magnitude of their resultant is:

solution.explanation: For two vectors of magnitudes A and B inclined at θ, the resultant has magnitude R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ).
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 N is the simple sum, valid only for θ = 0°. √34 N is the result for perpendicular forces (cos 90° = 0). √19 N uses −2AB cos θ, the formula for the magnitude of the difference of the vectors.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', addition of vectors: analytical method

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball is projected from level ground with a speed of 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, its time of flight is:

solution.concept: Time of flight of a projectile
solution.explanation: The vertical motion alone decides the time of flight: the vertical velocity u sin θ is reversed by gravity, so T = 2u sin θ / g.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 s is the time to reach the highest point (half the flight). 4 s uses 2u/g, ignoring the angle. 2√3 s uses cos θ, the horizontal component, in place of sin θ.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A particle moves along a straight line with uniform acceleration a. Its velocity is u at t = 0 and v at time t, and its displacement in this time is s. Match List-I (quantity) with List-II (expression).

List-I:
A. Velocity at time t
B. Displacement in time t
C. Square of the velocity after a displacement s
D. Average velocity over the time interval 0 to t

List-II:
I. u² + 2as
II. (u + v)/2
III. u + at
IV. ut + ½at²

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: For constant acceleration, v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as. Because velocity changes linearly with time, the average velocity is the mean of the initial and final velocities, (u + v)/2.
steps: Velocity at time t: u + at → III
Average velocity = (u + v)/2 → II (true only for uniform acceleration)
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the displacement formula with the average velocity, or the time-free relation with the average velocity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', kinematic equations for uniformly accelerated motion
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle moves along a circular track of radius r. When it has gone round exactly half the circle, the ratio of the distance it has travelled to the magnitude of its displacement is:

solution.explanation: Distance is the length of the path actually covered; displacement is the straight-line separation between the initial and final positions. After half a circle the particle is at the diametrically opposite point.
solution.why_others_wrong: π takes the displacement as r instead of 2r. 2/π is the ratio inverted. 1 would need a straight-line path.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', position, path length and displacement

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The angle between the vectors A = î + ĵ and B = ĵ + k̂ is:

solution.concept: Angle between two vectors from the scalar product
solution.explanation: A · B = AB cos θ, so cos θ = (A · B)/(AB). Compute the scalar product component by component and divide by the product of the magnitudes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 45° comes from taking cos θ = 1/√2 (dividing by only one magnitude). 90° assumes vectors along different axes are perpendicular, but they share the ĵ component. 30° confuses cos θ = ½ with sin θ = ½.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the scalar product

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball thrown vertically upward returns to the thrower's hand 6 s later. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, the maximum height it reaches above the hand is:

solution.concept: Symmetry of vertical motion under gravity
solution.explanation: Without air resistance the time of ascent equals the time of descent, each 3 s here. The ball falls freely from the top for 3 s, so H = ½g(3)².
steps: Time of ascent = 6/2 = 3 s → u = g t = 30 m/s
solution.why_others_wrong: 180 m treats the whole 6 s as the fall time. 90 m uses u²/g, dropping the factor 2. 30 m confuses the launch speed (30 m/s) with the height.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', kinematic equations for uniformly accelerated motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A car starts from rest and moves along a straight road. It accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 10 s, then moves at constant velocity for 10 s, and then decelerates uniformly to rest in 5 s. Its average speed for the whole journey is:

solution.explanation: The velocity–time graph is a trapezium. The distance is the area under it, and the average speed is the total distance divided by the total time.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 m/s averages the initial and maximum speeds, which is valid only for a single uniformly accelerated stage. 17.5 m/s divides by 20 s, leaving out the braking time. 20 m/s is the maximum speed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', acceleration (area under the v–t graph)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): From the same height above level ground, one ball is dropped from rest and another is thrown horizontally at the same instant. Neglecting air resistance, both reach the ground at the same time.
Reason (R): The horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent of each other, and the horizontal throw gives the second ball no initial vertical velocity.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration g. Their horizontal velocities differ, but horizontal motion does not affect vertical motion, so they fall the same height in the same time.
steps: Vertical motion of each: y = ½gt² with zero initial vertical velocity → same time of fall
R states the independence of the two motions and the zero vertical velocity, which is exactly why A holds
solution.why_others_wrong: R is not just true but is the reason: if the horizontal motion affected the vertical motion, the fall times would differ.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle starts from rest and moves along a straight line with a uniform acceleration of 2 m/s². After some time it begins to decelerate uniformly at 4 m/s² and comes to rest. The whole motion lasts 9 s. The maximum velocity reached by the particle is:

solution.explanation: If the peak velocity is v, the accelerating phase lasts v/a₁ and the decelerating phase lasts v/a₂. Their sum is the total time.
steps: Check: 6 s accelerating (2 × 6 = 12) and 3 s decelerating (12/4 = 3); 6 + 3 = 9 s ✓
solution.shortcut: t = v(1/a₁ + 1/a₂) → v = t·a₁a₂/(a₁ + a₂) = 9 × 8/6 = 12 m/s.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 m/s is the average velocity (half the peak) over the motion. 18 m/s takes 2 m/s² acting for the full 9 s. 36 m/s takes 4 m/s² for the full 9 s.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', kinematic equations for uniformly accelerated motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A projectile is launched from level ground with a speed of 20√2 m/s at 45° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, its speed 3 s after launch is:

solution.concept: Velocity of a projectile at an instant
solution.explanation: The horizontal component stays u cos θ; the vertical component becomes u sin θ − gt. The speed is the magnitude of their vector sum. The time of flight is 2u sin θ/g = 4 s, so at 3 s the projectile is still in the air, on its way down.
steps: At t = 3 s: v_y = 20 − 10 × 3 = −10 m/s (downward), vₓ = 20 m/s
solution.shortcut: At t = 3 s the projectile is as far past the top (t = 2 s) as it was before the top at t = 1 s, so the speeds at 1 s and 3 s are equal.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 m/s is only the vertical component. 20 m/s is only the horizontal component (the speed at the top). 10√29 m/s adds gt to the upward velocity, a sign error.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct? Neglect air resistance.

(a) For a particle in uniform circular motion, the velocity and the acceleration are perpendicular to each other at every instant.
(b) For a particle in uniform circular motion, the angular speed remains constant.
(c) For a projectile, the velocity and the acceleration are perpendicular to each other at the highest point of its path.
(d) For a particle in uniform circular motion on a circle of fixed radius, doubling the speed doubles the centripetal acceleration.
(e) The path of a projectile is a parabola only when it is launched at 45° to the horizontal.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Uniform circular motion and projectile motion
solution.explanation: In uniform circular motion the acceleration v²/r points to the centre while the velocity is tangential, and the angular speed v/r is constant. At the top of a projectile's path the velocity is horizontal and g is vertical. The centripetal acceleration v²/r varies as the square of the speed, and every projectile (any angle other than 90°) follows a parabola.
steps: (b) ω = v/r with v and r constant → true
(c) At the top the velocity is horizontal, g is vertical → true
(d) a = v²/r → doubling v makes a four times → false
(e) y = x tan θ − gx²/(2u²cos²θ) is a parabola for every θ → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Codes containing (d) forget that a ∝ v²; codes containing (e) confuse the angle of maximum range with the condition for a parabolic path.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion and uniform circular motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a particle moving along a straight line with constant acceleration, its average speed over any time interval equals the magnitude of its average velocity over that interval.
Statement II: For a particle moving along a straight line with constant acceleration, its average velocity over any time interval equals the mean of its velocities at the start and at the end of that interval.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Average speed and average velocity in uniformly accelerated motion
solution.explanation: With constant acceleration, velocity changes linearly with time, so the average velocity is (v₁ + v₂)/2. But if the velocity reverses during the interval (for example a ball thrown up and caught again), the path length exceeds the magnitude of the displacement, so the average speed exceeds |average velocity|.
steps: Statement I: counter-example — a ball thrown up at 10 m/s and caught 2 s later (g = 10 m/s²): average velocity 0, average speed 10 m/s → false
Statement II: v is linear in t → average velocity = (v₁ + v₂)/2 → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I holds only if the particle does not reverse its direction during the interval; constant acceleration does not guarantee that.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', average velocity and average speed
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The linear momentum of a body moving in a straight line increases steadily from 10 kg m/s to 30 kg m/s in 4 s. The force acting on it is:

solution.concept: Newton's second law in terms of momentum
solution.explanation: Force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = Δp/Δt. A steady change means the force is constant.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.5 N divides the final momentum, not the change, by the time. 80 N multiplies the change by the time instead of dividing. 2.5 N divides the initial momentum by the time.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's second law of motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body of mass 2 kg lies on a smooth horizontal surface. Two horizontal forces act on it: 6 N towards the east and 8 N towards the north. The magnitude of its acceleration is:

solution.concept: Second law with the vector sum of forces
solution.explanation: Acceleration is produced by the net (vector) force. Perpendicular forces combine by Pythagoras' theorem.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 m/s² adds the forces as numbers (14 N). 1 m/s² subtracts them (2 N). 10 m/s² is the net force in newtons not divided by the mass.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's second law of motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A body can remain at rest even when several forces act on it.
Reason (R): A body at rest has no force acting on it.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: A body stays at rest (or in uniform motion) when the vector sum of all the forces on it is zero; the forces themselves need not be zero. A book on a table has its weight and the normal reaction acting on it, and they balance.
steps: A: true — e.g. weight and normal reaction on a book at rest
R: false — a body at rest needs zero net force, not zero forces
solution.why_others_wrong: R confuses 'no net force' with 'no force'; A is a direct consequence of the correct idea.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', equilibrium of a particle
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (law or theorem) with List-II (its content).

List-I:
A. Newton's first law
B. Newton's second law
C. Newton's third law
D. Impulse–momentum theorem

List-II:
I. Forces always occur in pairs; the force of A on B is equal and opposite to the force of B on A
II. The rate of change of momentum of a body is proportional to the applied force and is in its direction
III. A body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless an external force acts on it
IV. The product of a force and the time for which it acts equals the change in momentum it produces

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: The first law describes inertia, the second law relates force to the rate of change of momentum, the third law describes action–reaction pairs, and the impulse–momentum theorem follows from the second law: FΔt = Δp.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the first and second laws, or treat the second law and the impulse theorem as the same statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's first, second and third laws; impulse
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A horse pulls a cart along a level road, and the horse and cart speed up together. The horizontal force that makes the horse accelerate forward is the force exerted by:

solution.concept: Newton's third law and the forces on a single body
solution.explanation: Consider the forces acting on the horse alone. The cart pulls the horse backward. The horse pushes the ground backward with its hooves, and by the third law the ground pushes the horse forward through friction. The horse accelerates forward because this forward push of the ground is larger than the backward pull of the cart.
steps: Forces on the horse (horizontal): ground → forward; cart → backward
Net forward force on the horse comes from the ground
solution.why_others_wrong: The cart's force on the horse points backward. The horse's force on the cart acts on the cart, not on the horse. The horse's force on the ground acts on the ground. A force on another body cannot accelerate the horse.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's third law of motion
solution.final_answer: Option C: The ground on the horse

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Circular motion: level and banked roads
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A vehicle can go round a banked curve at a certain speed even if the road is perfectly frictionless.
Reason (R): On a banked road, the horizontal component of the normal reaction points towards the centre of the curve and can supply the centripetal force.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: On a road banked at θ the normal reaction is tilted towards the centre of the curve. Its vertical component balances the weight and its horizontal component N sin θ provides mv²/r. At the speed v₀ = √(rg tan θ) no friction is needed at all.
steps: N cos θ = mg and N sin θ = mv₀²/r → v₀² = rg tan θ
R gives the source of the centripetal force when friction is absent, which is exactly why A is possible
solution.why_others_wrong: Both are true, and R is the physical reason for A, so the first option is the answer.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', circular motion (motion of a car on a banked road)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A certain force gives a body of mass m₁ an acceleration of 6 m/s² and a body of mass m₂ an acceleration of 3 m/s². If the two bodies are tied together, the same force gives the combination an acceleration of:

solution.concept: Second law for a combined mass
solution.explanation: Write each mass in terms of the force: m₁ = F/6 and m₂ = F/3. The combination has mass m₁ + m₂ = F/2, so the same force gives it an acceleration F/(F/2).
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.5 m/s² averages the accelerations. 9 m/s² adds them. 3 m/s² takes the smaller acceleration, as if the lighter body added nothing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's second law of motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A bullet of mass 50 g moving at 200 m/s enters a fixed wooden block and comes to rest after penetrating 10 cm. Assuming the resistive force of the wood is constant, its magnitude is:

solution.concept: Constant retarding force from v² = u² − 2as
solution.explanation: Find the uniform retardation from the stopping distance, then multiply by the mass.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 × 10⁴ N drops the factor 2 in v² = 2as. 1.0 × 10³ N takes the distance as 1 m (cm-to-m slip). 1.0 × 10² N divides the momentum by the distance, which is not a force.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's second law of motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The static friction acting on a body can be in the direction of the body's motion.
Statement II: For a given pair of surfaces, the limiting value of static friction does not depend on the normal reaction between them.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Direction and magnitude of static friction
solution.explanation: Static friction opposes impending relative motion between the surfaces, not the motion of the body. A box resting on the floor of a truck that is speeding up is carried forward by static friction, which then acts in the direction of motion. The limiting static friction is μₛN, directly proportional to the normal reaction.
steps: Statement I: box on an accelerating truck — friction forward, along the motion → true
Statement II: f_max = μₛN depends on N → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II states the area-independence law wrongly; friction is independent of the area of contact, not of the normal reaction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform rope of mass 2 kg and length 4 m lies straight on a smooth horizontal floor. One end is pulled horizontally along the rope with a force of 10 N. The tension in the rope at a point 1 m from the pulled end is:

solution.concept: Tension in a rope that has mass
solution.explanation: A massive rope accelerates with the force applied, so its tension falls along its length. The tension at a point is the force needed to accelerate the part of the rope behind that point.
steps: Acceleration of the whole rope: a = 10/2 = 5 m/s²
Part behind the point: length 3 m → mass 2 × 3/4 = 1.5 kg
solution.shortcut: T(x) = F(1 − x/L) with x measured from the pulled end: 10 × 3/4 = 7.5 N.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 N treats the rope as massless (uniform tension). 2.5 N is the force needed by the 1 m piece in front, not the 3 m behind. 5 N is the tension at the midpoint.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's second law of motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 10 kg hangs at rest from two light strings tied to a horizontal ceiling. One string makes an angle of 30° with the ceiling and the other makes an angle of 60° with the ceiling. Taking g = 10 m/s², the tension in the string that makes 60° with the ceiling is:

solution.explanation: The weight and the two tensions meet at the knot. For equilibrium, the horizontal components of the tensions cancel and their vertical components add up to the weight.
steps: Horizontal: T₁ cos 30° = T₂ cos 60° → T₂ = √3 T₁
Vertical: T₁ sin 30° + T₂ sin 60° = 100 → T₁/2 + 3T₁/2 = 100 → T₁ = 50 N
solution.shortcut: The two strings are perpendicular (30° + 60° = 90°), so T₂ = mg sin 60° = 50√3 N and T₁ = mg cos 60°.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 N is the tension in the other (30°) string. 100 N assumes one string carries the whole weight. 100/√3 N comes from resolving with sine and cosine interchanged.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', equilibrium of a particle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A machine gun fires 600 bullets per minute, each of mass 20 g, with a speed of 500 m/s relative to the ground. The average force needed to hold the gun in place is:

solution.concept: Force as the rate of change of momentum
solution.explanation: Each second the gun gives a definite amount of forward momentum to the bullets; by the third law it receives an equal backward momentum each second, which must be cancelled by the holding force.
steps: Momentum given per second = 10 × 0.020 × 500 = 100 kg m/s per s
solution.why_others_wrong: 6000 N uses 600 bullets per second (minutes not converted). 10 N is the momentum of a single bullet. 50 N halves the answer with no physical reason.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's second law of motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Circular motion: level and banked roads
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about vehicles taking circular turns on roads are correct?

(a) On a level road, the maximum speed at which a car can take a turn of radius r without skidding is √(μₛrg), whatever the mass of the car.
(b) On a road banked at a given angle, friction allows a maximum safe speed greater than the speed at which no friction is needed.
(c) A car cannot take a circular turn on a perfectly frictionless level road.
(d) When a car takes a turn at constant speed on a level road, the friction on its tyres acts opposite to its velocity.
(e) The speed at which a car can take a banked turn without needing friction depends on the mass of the car.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Friction and banking in circular motion
solution.explanation: On a level road static friction alone supplies mv²/r, so mv²/r ≤ μₛmg and v_max = √(μₛrg): the mass cancels. On a banked road friction can act down the slope and add to the centripetal component, raising the maximum speed above v₀ = √(rg tan θ), which is also mass-independent. With no friction on a level road nothing horizontal acts towards the centre. At constant speed the friction is radial (towards the centre), not along the velocity.
steps: (a) μₛmg ≥ mv²/r → v_max = √(μₛrg), independent of m → true
(b) v_max = √[rg(μₛ + tan θ)/(1 − μₛ tan θ)] > √(rg tan θ) → true
(c) No horizontal force towards the centre → true
(d) Friction is centripetal (perpendicular to v) at constant speed → false
(e) v₀ = √(rg tan θ), independent of m → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Codes containing (d) think of friction as always opposing motion; codes containing (e) forget that the mass cancels on both sides of the equations.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', circular motion (level and banked roads)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two bodies of masses 1 kg and 4 kg have equal kinetic energies. The ratio of the magnitude of the linear momentum of the 1 kg body to that of the 4 kg body is:

solution.concept: Relation between kinetic energy and momentum
solution.explanation: K = p²/2m, so p = √(2mK). For equal K, p ∝ √m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 4 takes p ∝ m. 2 : 1 inverts the correct ratio (that is the ratio of speeds). 1 : 16 squares the mass ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', kinetic energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Work by constant and variable force
questions.question_text: Which of the following is a conservative force?

solution.explanation: A force is conservative if the work it does between two points does not depend on the path, so that it can be derived from a potential energy. Gravity (and the spring force) are conservative; friction, drag and viscous forces dissipate mechanical energy and are non-conservative.
steps: Work done by gravity = −mg(h₂ − h₁), path-independent → conservative
Friction, drag and viscosity always remove mechanical energy → non-conservative
solution.why_others_wrong: Kinetic friction, air resistance and viscous force all do negative work that depends on the length of the path, so none of them has a potential energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', conservative forces and conservation of mechanical energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Work by constant and variable force
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A potential energy can be defined only for a conservative force.
Statement II: The work done by the gravitational force on a body moving from one point to another near the Earth's surface does not depend on the path followed.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Potential energy is defined through the work done by a force, and this definition is meaningful only when the work is the same for every path between two points — that is, for a conservative force. Gravity is such a force: its work depends only on the change in height.
steps: Statement I: V(x) needs path-independent work → true
Statement II: W_g = −mgΔh for any path → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true; neither contains the usual traps (friction having potential energy, or gravity's work depending on the path).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the concept of potential energy
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball of mass 1 kg is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m and reaches the ground with a speed of 18 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², the work done on the ball by air resistance during the fall is:

solution.concept: Work–energy theorem with a non-conservative force
solution.explanation: The total work done by all forces equals the change in kinetic energy. Gravity does +mgh; the rest of the change is due to air resistance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 38 J has the wrong sign: air resistance opposes the motion and does negative work. −162 J takes the whole kinetic energy as lost. −362 J adds the two energies instead of subtracting.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the work-energy theorem

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A spring of spring constant 400 N/m is already stretched by 5 cm from its natural length. The work needed to stretch it further, so that its extension becomes 10 cm, is:

solution.concept: Work done in stretching a spring
solution.explanation: The work done against the spring force equals the increase in its elastic potential energy, ½kx², between the two extensions.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.5 J uses ½k(x₂ − x₁)², as if the spring started unstretched. 2.0 J ignores the initial stretch. 2.5 J adds the two energies.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the potential energy of a spring

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small bob of mass 0.2 kg hangs from a light inextensible string. The bob is pulled aside until the string is horizontal and taut, and is then released from rest. Taking g = 10 m/s², the tension in the string as the bob passes through its lowest point is:

solution.concept: Energy conservation with the centripetal force equation
solution.explanation: Energy conservation gives the speed at the bottom; at the bottom the net upward force T − mg supplies the centripetal force mv²/L. The length of the string cancels.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 N is just the weight (no centripetal term). 4 N is mv²/L alone, forgetting to add the weight. 10 N (5mg) is the tension at the lowest point when the bob just completes a full vertical circle, a different motion.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', conservation of mechanical energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a one-dimensional elastic collision between two bodies, the kinetic energy of each body is the same after the collision as before it.
Reason (R): In an elastic collision, the total kinetic energy of the colliding bodies after the collision is equal to that before the collision.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: What is conserved in an elastic collision
solution.explanation: Elastic means the total kinetic energy of the system is conserved, not the kinetic energy of each body. Kinetic energy is usually transferred from one body to the other; for example, a moving ball striking an identical ball at rest stops and gives all its kinetic energy to the other.
steps: A: equal masses, one at rest — velocities exchange, so each body's KE changes → false
R: definition of an elastic collision → true
solution.why_others_wrong: A wrongly applies to each body a conservation law that holds only for the system.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', collisions
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A constant net force acts on a body of mass 2 kg, initially at rest, and gives it a speed of 10 m/s in 5 s. The instantaneous power delivered by the force at the end of the 5 s is:

solution.explanation: With a constant force the speed rises steadily, so the power Fv also rises steadily. The instantaneous power at the end is twice the average power over the interval.
steps: Check: average power = ΔK/t = 100/5 = 20 W = half the final power ✓
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 W is the average power over the 5 s. 100 W is the kinetic energy gained (in joules), not a rate. 8 W multiplies the force by the acceleration.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 12.5 m onto a hard horizontal floor. At each impact it loses 36% of the kinetic energy it has just before the impact. Neglecting air resistance, the maximum height it reaches after the second impact is:

solution.concept: Energy loss in successive inelastic impacts
solution.explanation: Without air resistance, the kinetic energy just before an impact equals mg × (height fallen), and the height reached after the impact is proportional to the kinetic energy kept. Each impact keeps 64% of the energy, so each rebound height is 0.64 of the previous one.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8.0 m is the height after only the first impact. 3.5 m subtracts 36% of the original height twice instead of compounding. 1.62 m keeps 36% at each impact instead of losing 36%.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', collisions and conservation of mechanical energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The work done by the net force on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.
(b) Power is a vector quantity, because it is the product of force and velocity.
(c) The kinetic energy of a body can never be negative.
(d) If the linear momentum of a body increases by 100%, its kinetic energy also increases by 100%.
(e) The work done by kinetic friction on a block sliding over a fixed rough floor is negative.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: The work–energy theorem relates the net work to ΔK. Power is the scalar product F · v, so it is a scalar. K = ½mv² can never be negative. K = p²/2m, so doubling p multiplies K by 4 (an increase of 300%). On a fixed floor, kinetic friction acts opposite to the block's displacement, so its work is negative.
steps: (b) P = F · v is a scalar → false
(d) p → 2p gives K → 4K, a 300% increase → false
(e) friction opposite to displacement → W < 0 → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Codes containing (b) treat a dot product as a vector; codes containing (d) assume K ∝ p instead of K ∝ p².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', work-energy theorem and power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wheel starts from rest and rotates about a fixed axis with a uniform angular acceleration of 2 rad/s². The angle through which it turns in the first 5 s is:

solution.concept: Kinematics of rotation with constant angular acceleration
solution.explanation: The rotational equations have the same form as the linear ones: θ = ω₀t + ½αt².
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 rad is the final angular velocity αt in rad/s. 50 rad drops the factor ½. 12.5 rad uses ¼αt².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', kinematics of rotational motion about a fixed axis

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text: Two small balls of masses 1 kg and 2 kg are fixed to a light rigid rod at distances of 0.5 m and 1.0 m respectively from an axis perpendicular to the rod. The moment of inertia of the system about this axis is:

solution.concept: Moment of inertia of point masses
solution.explanation: For point masses, I = Σ mᵢrᵢ², where rᵢ is the perpendicular distance of each mass from the axis.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.5 kg m² uses Σmr without squaring the distances. 3.0 kg m² puts both masses at 1 m. 0.75 kg m² puts both masses at 0.5 m.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', moment of inertia

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, with moment of inertia I and angular velocity ω about that axis, match List-I (quantity) with List-II (expression). τ is a constant torque about the axis.

List-I:
A. Rotational kinetic energy
B. Angular momentum about the axis
C. Power delivered by the torque
D. Work done by the torque in turning the body through an angle θ

List-II:
I. τθ
II. ½Iω²
III. τω
IV. Iω

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Replace m by I, v by ω, F by τ and x by θ in the linear formulas: K = ½mv² → ½Iω²; p = mv → L = Iω; P = Fv → τω; W = Fx → τθ.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap kinetic energy with angular momentum, or power with work.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', work done by a torque; angular momentum in case of rotation about a fixed axis
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The angular momentum of a particle about a point is the moment, about that point, of the particle's:

solution.explanation: Angular momentum of a particle about a point O is l = r × p, where r is its position vector from O and p its linear momentum. In the same way, torque τ = r × F is the moment of force.
steps: l = r × p → moment of linear momentum
τ = r × F → moment of force (that is torque, not angular momentum)
solution.why_others_wrong: The moment of a force is torque. Kinetic energy and mass are scalars; a 'moment' is defined through the vector product r × (vector).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', angular momentum of a particle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A disc of moment of inertia 0.2 kg m² is rotating at 10 rad/s about a fixed axis. A constant braking torque brings it to rest in 4 s. The magnitude of the braking torque is:

solution.concept: Torque as the rate of change of angular momentum
solution.explanation: For rotation about a fixed axis, τ = dL/dt. A constant torque changes L = Iω uniformly.
steps: Initial L = Iω = 0.2 × 10 = 2.0 kg m²/s; final L = 0
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 N m is the initial angular momentum, not divided by the time. 8.0 N m multiplies by the time. 0.25 N m uses half the change in angular momentum.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', angular momentum in case of rotation about a fixed axis

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A flywheel of moment of inertia 2 kg m² rotates about its axis at 600 revolutions per minute. Its rotational kinetic energy is:

solution.explanation: Convert the rotation rate to angular velocity in rad/s (ω = 2πf, with f in revolutions per second), then use K = ½Iω².
solution.why_others_wrong: 100π² J uses ω = πf (forgetting the 2 in 2πf). 3.6 × 10⁵ J uses ω = 600 rad/s with no conversion. 40π J is the angular momentum Iω, not the energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', kinematics of rotational motion; rotational kinetic energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The angular momentum of a particle moving with constant velocity along a straight line is constant about any fixed point.
Reason (R): No net force acts on a particle moving with constant velocity, so the torque on it about any fixed point is zero.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Torque and conservation of angular momentum of a particle
solution.explanation: dl/dt = τ = r × F. With F = 0 the torque about every fixed point is zero, so l = r × p stays constant. Geometrically, |l| = p × (perpendicular distance of the line from the point), and both factors are constant.
steps: F = 0 → τ = r × F = 0 about any point
Check: |l| = p d⊥, with p and d⊥ fixed
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the reason for A: zero torque is exactly the condition for angular momentum to be conserved.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', torque and angular momentum
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A rigid body in rotational equilibrium must be at rest.
Statement II: The torque of a force about a point is zero if the line of action of the force passes through that point.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Rotational equilibrium means zero net torque, so the angular momentum is constant: a body rotating at a constant angular velocity (a freely spinning wheel with no friction) is in rotational equilibrium without being at rest. Torque τ = rF sin θ = F × (perpendicular distance of the line of action from the point), which is zero when the line passes through the point.
steps: Statement I: zero net torque allows uniform rotation → false
Statement II: perpendicular distance r⊥ = 0 → τ = 0 → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I confuses equilibrium (zero net torque) with rest, just as translational equilibrium allows uniform motion.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', equilibrium of a rigid body
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about moment of inertia are correct?

(a) The theorem of parallel axes applies to a body of any shape.
(b) The theorem of perpendicular axes applies to three-dimensional bodies of any shape.
(c) The moment of inertia of a body depends on the position and orientation of the axis of rotation.
(d) The moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod about an axis perpendicular to it through one end is four times its moment of inertia about a parallel axis through its centre.
(e) The moment of inertia of a uniform disc about a diameter is greater than about the axis through its centre perpendicular to its plane.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Theorems of parallel and perpendicular axes
solution.explanation: The parallel axes theorem I = I_cm + Md² holds for any body. The perpendicular axes theorem I_z = I_x + I_y holds only for a planar body (lamina). For a rod, I_end = ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/3, four times ML²/12. For a disc, the perpendicular axes theorem gives I_diameter = ½ × MR²/2 = MR²/4, which is less than MR²/2.
steps: (c) true — I depends on the axis
solution.why_others_wrong: Codes containing (b) extend the perpendicular axes theorem beyond plane bodies; codes containing (e) reverse the two moments of inertia of the disc.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', theorems of perpendicular and parallel axes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: From a uniform circular disc of radius R, a circular hole of radius R/2 is cut out. The edge of the hole touches the rim of the disc, so the centre of the hole is at a distance R/2 from the centre O of the original disc. The centre of mass of the remaining part is at a distance from O of:

options.text: R/8, on the side opposite to the hole
R/3, on the side opposite to the hole
R/6, on the side opposite to the hole
R/6, on the same side as the hole

solution.concept: Centre of mass of a body with a part removed
solution.explanation: Treat the remaining part as the full disc minus the removed disc. The mass of a uniform disc is proportional to its area, so the hole has a quarter of the mass. Taking O as origin, the full disc's centre of mass is at O.
steps: Mass of hole = M/4 (area ratio (R/2)²/R² = 1/4); remaining mass = 3M/4
The centre of mass is R/6 from O, on the side away from the hole
solution.why_others_wrong: R/8 divides by the full mass M instead of the remaining 3M/4. R/3 places the centre of the hole at a distance R from O instead of R/2. R/6 on the same side gets the sign wrong: removing mass shifts the centre of mass away from the hole.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', centre of mass
solution.final_answer: Option C: R/6, on the side opposite to the hole

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform rod of mass 0.9 kg and length 1.0 m lies at rest on a smooth horizontal table. It is pivoted at its centre so that it can rotate freely about a fixed vertical axis. A small lump of putty of mass 0.1 kg, moving horizontally at 10 m/s perpendicular to the rod, strikes one end of the rod and sticks to it. The angular velocity of the rod just after the impact is:

solution.concept: Conservation of angular momentum about a fixed axis
solution.explanation: During the short impact the pivot exerts a force, so linear momentum is not conserved; but that force passes through the axis and has no torque about it, so angular momentum about the axis is conserved.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20/3 rad/s leaves out the putty's own moment of inertia after it sticks. 2 rad/s conserves linear momentum, which the pivot force does not allow. 10 rad/s comes from ω = v/L with no conservation law at all.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', conservation of angular momentum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform rod of length 1.5 m is hinged at one end so that it can rotate freely in a vertical plane about a horizontal axis through the hinge. It is held horizontal and then released. Taking g = 10 m/s², its angular acceleration just after release is:

solution.concept: τ = Iα about a fixed axis
solution.explanation: Just after release the angular velocity is zero, and the only torque about the hinge is that of the weight, acting at the centre of mass at L/2 from the hinge. The moment of inertia about the end is ML²/3.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20/3 rad/s² is g/L, treating the rod as a point mass at its far end. 20 rad/s² (3g/L) puts the weight at the far end. 40 rad/s² uses ML²/12, the moment of inertia about the centre, instead of about the hinge.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', dynamics of rotational motion about a fixed axis

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) If the angular acceleration α is constant, the angular velocity at time t is ω = ω₀ + αt.
(b) The angular velocity vector is directed along the axis of rotation.
(c) All particles of the body have the same centripetal acceleration.
(d) If its angular momentum about the axis is L, its rotational kinetic energy is L²/2I.
(e) If no external torque acts and the body's moment of inertia about the axis is halved (by redistributing its mass), its rotational kinetic energy also halves.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Kinematics and dynamics of fixed-axis rotation
solution.explanation: The rotational kinematic equations mirror the linear ones, and ω points along the axis (right-hand rule). Every particle has the same ω but the centripetal acceleration ω²r depends on its distance r from the axis. K = ½Iω² = L²/2I. With no external torque L is constant, so halving I doubles K (the extra energy comes from the internal work done in pulling the mass inward).
steps: (e) L fixed, I → I/2 gives K = L²/2I → doubles → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Codes containing (c) confuse equal angular velocity with equal centripetal acceleration; codes containing (e) forget that L, not ω, stays fixed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', rotational motion about a fixed axis; conservation of angular momentum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A planet has half the mass and half the radius of the Earth. If g is the acceleration due to gravity on the Earth's surface, the acceleration due to gravity on the planet's surface is:

solution.explanation: At the surface of a spherical body, g = GM/R². Scale the mass and the square of the radius.
solution.why_others_wrong: g assumes the two halvings cancel (they would only if g ∝ M/R). g/2 ignores the radius. 4g ignores the mass.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', acceleration due to gravity of the earth

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The value of the universal gravitational constant G was first determined experimentally by:

solution.concept: History of the measurement of G
solution.explanation: Newton stated the law of gravitation but did not measure G. The English scientist Henry Cavendish measured it in 1798 with a torsion balance, using the tiny attraction between lead spheres.
steps: G was measured in a laboratory with a torsion balance by Cavendish (1798)
solution.why_others_wrong: Kepler found the laws of planetary motion from Tycho Brahe's observations; Newton proposed the law of gravitation. None of them measured G.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', the gravitational constant

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (quantity) with List-II (its SI unit).

List-I:
A. Universal gravitational constant G
B. Gravitational potential
C. Gravitational field intensity
D. Gravitational potential energy

List-II:
I. J
II. N kg⁻¹
III. N m² kg⁻²
IV. J kg⁻¹

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: From F = Gm₁m₂/r², G = Fr²/(m₁m₂) has unit N m² kg⁻². Potential is potential energy per unit mass (J kg⁻¹), field intensity is force per unit mass (N kg⁻¹, equivalent to m s⁻²), and potential energy is in joules.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange potential (energy per mass) and field (force per mass), or potential and potential energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', universal law of gravitation; gravitational potential energy
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A planet moves round the Sun in an elliptical orbit. Its greatest distance from the Sun (at aphelion) is three times its least distance (at perihelion). The ratio of its speed at perihelion to its speed at aphelion is:

solution.concept: Conservation of angular momentum (Kepler's second law)
solution.explanation: The Sun's force on the planet is central, so the planet's angular momentum about the Sun is constant. At perihelion and aphelion the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so L = mvr at both points.
steps: m v_p r_p = m v_a r_a
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/3 inverts the ratio (the planet is fastest when nearest the Sun). 9 squares the distance ratio. √3 uses the circular-orbit relation v ∝ 1/√r, which does not apply to two points of the same ellipse.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', Kepler's laws

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Four particles, each of mass m, are placed at the corners of a square of side a. The gravitational potential at the centre of the square is (G is the universal gravitational constant):

solution.explanation: Potential is a scalar, so the potentials of the four masses simply add. Each corner is half a diagonal, a/√2, from the centre.
steps: Distance of each corner from the centre = a√2/2 = a/√2
solution.why_others_wrong: −4Gm/a takes the distance as a. −2√2 Gm/a takes it as the full diagonal a√2. Zero is the gravitational field at the centre (the vector contributions cancel), not the potential, which is a scalar and never cancels.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', gravitational potential energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The escape speed of a body from the Earth's surface is vₑ. Neglecting the Earth's rotation and the atmosphere, the escape speed of a body from a point at a height 3R above the surface (R = radius of the Earth) is:

solution.concept: Escape speed from a point at distance r from the Earth's centre
solution.explanation: To escape from a point at distance r from the centre, ½mv² must equal GMm/r, so v = √(2GM/r) ∝ 1/√r. The distance from the centre here is R + 3R = 4R.
solution.why_others_wrong: vₑ/√3 uses the height 3R instead of the distance 4R from the centre. vₑ/4 takes v ∝ 1/r. vₑ/√2 would be the answer at a height R.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', escape speed

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a body is moved farther away from the Earth, the gravitational potential energy of the body–Earth system increases.
Reason (R): The gravitational force is attractive, so an external agent must do positive work against it to increase the separation slowly.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: The change in potential energy equals the work done by an external agent moving the body slowly (without change in kinetic energy). Because gravity pulls the body back, that work is positive when the separation increases, so U = −GMm/r rises towards zero.
steps: U = −GMm/r: r larger → U less negative → U increases
ΔU = W_external > 0 since gravity is attractive
solution.why_others_wrong: R gives the physical reason for A, so both are true and R explains A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', gravitational potential energy
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body is released from rest at a height above the Earth's surface equal to the Earth's radius R. Neglect air resistance and the Earth's rotation, and take R = 6400 km and g = 10 m/s² at the surface. The speed with which it strikes the Earth's surface is:

solution.explanation: Over a fall comparable to R, g is not constant, so use U = −GMm/r instead of mgh, together with GM = gR².
steps: Loss of PE = GMm/R − GMm/2R = GMm/2R = mgR/2
solution.why_others_wrong: 11.3 km/s uses v = √(2gR), treating g as constant over the whole height R. 5.7 km/s is √(gR/2). 4.0 km/s halves the correct speed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', gravitational potential energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Taking the Earth's radius as 6400 km and ignoring its rotation, the height above the Earth's surface at which the acceleration due to gravity becomes 64% of its value at the surface is:

solution.concept: Exact variation of g with height
solution.explanation: g(h) = g R²/(R + h)². The approximation g(1 − 2h/R) is valid only for h ≪ R; a 36% drop in g is far outside that range, so the exact expression must be used.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1152 km uses the small-height formula 1 − 2h/R = 0.64, which is not valid for so large a change. 3200 km is R/2. 2304 km uses 1 − h/R = 0.64.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', acceleration due to gravity below and above the surface of earth

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct? Take the gravitational potential to be zero at infinity, and treat the Earth as a uniform sphere.

(a) The gravitational potential at a point is the work done by an external agent, per unit mass, in bringing a body slowly from infinity to that point.
(b) The gravitational potential everywhere inside a uniform thin spherical shell is zero.
(c) The gravitational field everywhere inside a uniform thin spherical shell is zero.
(d) The acceleration due to gravity is greatest at the centre of the Earth.
(e) For a height h much smaller than the Earth's radius, the increase in gravitational potential energy of a body of mass m raised through h from the surface is approximately mgh.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Inside a uniform thin shell the field is zero, so the potential does not change from point to point — it is constant at its surface value −GM/R, not zero. Inside a uniform Earth g = g₀(1 − d/R) decreases to zero at the centre. Near the surface the exact ΔU = GMm[1/R − 1/(R + h)] reduces to mgh for h ≪ R.
steps: (e) ΔU ≈ mgh for h ≪ R → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Codes containing (b) confuse zero field with zero potential; zero field only means the potential is constant. Codes containing (d) reverse the variation of g with depth.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', gravitational potential energy; acceleration due to gravity below the surface

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wire 2 m long is stretched so that its length increases by 1 mm. The longitudinal strain in the wire is:

solution.explanation: Longitudinal strain is the change in length divided by the original length, both in the same unit. It has no unit.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 × 10³ is L/ΔL, the ratio inverted. 5 × 10⁻¹ divides 1 (mm) by 2 (m) without converting units. 2 × 10⁻³ multiplies instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', stress and strain

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Water flows steadily through a pipe. At a section where the cross-sectional area is 4 cm², the speed of the water is 2 m/s. The speed at a narrower section of area 1 cm² is:

solution.explanation: For the steady flow of an incompressible liquid, the volume flowing past every cross-section per second is the same: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.5 m/s inverts the area ratio (the liquid must speed up where the pipe narrows). 4 m/s uses the square root of the area ratio, as if speed depended on the radius ratio. 32 m/s squares the area ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', streamline flow (equation of continuity)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A steel rail is 10 m long at 20 °C. The coefficient of linear expansion of steel is 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. The increase in its length when its temperature rises to 60 °C is:

solution.explanation: For a small temperature change, ΔL = αLΔT.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.48 mm and 48 mm slip a power of ten in converting metres to millimetres. 14.4 mm uses 3α, the coefficient of volume expansion.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', thermal expansion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The hydraulic brakes of an automobile work on the principle of:

solution.explanation: In hydraulic brakes, a small force on the pedal increases the pressure in the brake fluid. By Pascal's law this pressure is transmitted undiminished through the enclosed fluid to the wider pistons at the wheels, which therefore exert a much larger force on the brake pads.
steps: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of it → force multiplication
solution.why_others_wrong: Bernoulli's principle concerns flowing fluids, Archimedes' principle concerns buoyancy and Stokes' law gives the viscous drag on a moving sphere; none of them explains hydraulic brakes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', Pascal's law (hydraulic machines)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (law) with List-II (what it states).

List-I:
A. Stefan–Boltzmann law
B. Wien's displacement law
C. Newton's law of cooling
D. Hooke's law

List-II:
I. Within the elastic limit, stress is proportional to strain
II. The wavelength at which a black body emits most strongly, multiplied by its absolute temperature, is a constant
III. For a small temperature difference, the rate of loss of heat of a body is proportional to the difference between its temperature and that of its surroundings
IV. The energy radiated per unit time by a black body is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Laws of radiation, cooling and elasticity
solution.explanation: Stefan–Boltzmann: H ∝ T⁴. Wien: λₘT = constant. Newton's law of cooling: −dQ/dt ∝ (T − Tₛ) for small differences. Hooke's law: stress ∝ strain within the elastic limit.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the two radiation laws, or Newton's law of cooling with Wien's law.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', radiation and Newton's law of cooling; 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', Hooke's law
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: When the pressure on a liquid is increased by 1.0 × 10⁶ Pa, its volume decreases by 0.05%. The bulk modulus of the liquid is:

solution.explanation: Bulk modulus B = Δp/(ΔV/V), the pressure change divided by the magnitude of the fractional change in volume. A percentage must be divided by 100 to get the fraction.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 × 10⁷ Pa uses 0.05 as the fraction (percentage not divided by 100). 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ is the compressibility 1/B, with the wrong unit. 5 × 10² Pa multiplies the pressure by the volume strain.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', bulk modulus

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A U-tube open at both ends contains water. Some oil, which does not mix with water, is poured into one arm. In equilibrium the oil column stands 10 cm above the oil–water interface, while the water in the other arm stands 8 cm above the level of that interface. Taking the density of water as 1000 kg/m³, the density of the oil is:

solution.concept: Equal pressures at the same level in a liquid at rest
solution.explanation: Points at the same horizontal level in the same continuous liquid (water here) are at the same pressure. Take the level of the oil–water interface: above it, one arm has 10 cm of oil and the other 8 cm of water, both open to the atmosphere.
steps: P_atm + ρ_oil g (0.10) = P_atm + ρ_w g (0.08)
solution.why_others_wrong: 1250 kg/m³ inverts the height ratio; a lighter liquid needs the taller column. 1000 kg/m³ ignores the height difference. 200 kg/m³ uses the 2 cm difference in heights.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', variation of pressure with depth

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A flat plate of area 0.1 m² is moved at a steady speed of 0.2 m/s parallel to a fixed flat surface, separated from it by a 2 mm thick layer of a liquid of coefficient of viscosity 1.5 Pa s. Assuming the speed of the liquid changes uniformly across the layer, the force needed to keep the plate moving is:

solution.explanation: The viscous force is F = ηA(dv/dx). With a uniform velocity gradient across the layer, dv/dx = v/d.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5 N takes the layer as 2 cm thick. 0.015 N leaves the thickness as '2' without converting millimetres to metres. 1.5 × 10⁻³ N uses d/v instead of v/d.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', viscosity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The surface tension of a liquid is numerically equal to the surface energy per unit area of its free surface.
Statement II: Water does not spread on a waxy surface but forms drops, because the angle of contact between water and wax is obtuse.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Surface energy and angle of contact
solution.explanation: Increasing a liquid surface by area ΔA at constant temperature needs work SΔA, so the surface energy per unit area equals S (same dimensions, N/m = J/m²). When the cohesive forces in water exceed its adhesion to wax, the angle of contact is greater than 90° and water forms drops instead of wetting the surface.
steps: Statement I: W = SΔA → S = energy per unit area → true
Statement II: θ > 90° on a waxy (or oily) surface → water does not wet it → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true; the usual traps (surface tension as force per area, acute angle for non-wetting) do not appear.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', surface tension (surface energy, angle of contact)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): During a strong windstorm, a light roof can be lifted off a house even though the wind blows horizontally over it.
Reason (R): The fast-moving air above the roof is at a lower pressure than the nearly still air under the roof, as Bernoulli's principle predicts.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Dynamic lift from a pressure difference
solution.explanation: Along a streamline, p + ½ρv² is constant (for horizontal flow). Air moving fast over the roof has a lower pressure than the still air inside, so the pressure difference across the roof times its area gives a net upward force.
steps: p_inside − p_above ≈ ½ρv² > 0 → net upward force on the roof
R gives exactly the cause of A
solution.why_others_wrong: The roof is lifted because of the pressure difference that R describes, so R explains A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', Bernoulli's principle (dynamic lift)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Heat can be transferred by natural convection within a solid.
Statement II: Of conduction, convection and radiation, only radiation can transfer heat through a vacuum.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Convection is the transfer of heat by the actual motion of matter, which is possible only in fluids (liquids and gases); natural convection arises when heated, less dense fluid rises under gravity. Conduction and convection need a medium, while radiation is carried by electromagnetic waves and needs none — that is how the Sun's heat reaches the Earth.
steps: Statement I: the particles of a solid cannot flow → no convection → false
Statement II: radiation needs no medium → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is false because convection needs bulk movement of the material, which a solid does not allow.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', heat transfer
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: 10 g of steam at 100 °C is passed into 145 g of water at 20 °C kept in an insulated container of negligible heat capacity, and all the steam condenses. Take the latent heat of vaporisation of water as 540 cal g⁻¹ and its specific heat as 1 cal g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. The final temperature of the mixture is:

solution.concept: Principle of calorimetry with a change of state
solution.explanation: Heat given out by the steam (latent heat on condensing, then the heat released as the condensed water cools to the final temperature T) equals the heat taken in by the cold water.
steps: Check: all the steam condenses, since 145 g of water needs 145 × 80 = 11 600 cal to reach 100 °C, more than the 5400 cal of latent heat available
solution.why_others_wrong: 57.2 °C counts the latent heat but forgets the heat released as the condensed water cools from 100 °C. 25.2 °C ignores the latent heat and treats the steam as water at 100 °C. 100 °C would need far more steam.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', calorimetry and change of state

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A black body emits radiant energy at the rate E when its temperature is 27 °C. When its temperature is raised to 327 °C, it emits radiant energy at the rate:

solution.explanation: The energy radiated per unit time by a black body is σAT⁴, where T is the absolute temperature. Celsius temperatures must be converted to kelvin first.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2E takes the emitted power proportional to T. 8E uses T³. 2.1 × 10⁴ E uses the Celsius temperatures, (327/27)⁴.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', radiation (Stefan–Boltzmann law)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Heat flows at the rate H through a cylindrical rod whose ends are kept at two fixed temperatures; its sides are insulated. A second rod of the same material has twice the length and twice the radius. If its ends are kept at the same two temperatures, the rate of heat flow through it in the steady state is:

solution.explanation: In the steady state the rate of heat flow is H = KA(T₁ − T₂)/L. The cross-sectional area A = πr² grows as the square of the radius.
solution.why_others_wrong: H assumes doubling the radius and doubling the length cancel (they would only if H ∝ r/L). 4H ignores the longer length. H/2 makes H proportional to L/A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', conduction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about surface tension are correct?

(a) Soaps and detergents lower the surface tension of water.
(b) The force of surface tension acts along (tangential to) the liquid surface.
(c) Surface tension is a force per unit area of the liquid surface.
(d) The excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius r is twice the excess pressure inside a drop of the same soap solution of the same radius.
(e) A liquid rises in a capillary tube only if its angle of contact with the tube is obtuse.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Surface tension, excess pressure and capillarity
solution.explanation: Detergents reduce the surface tension of water, which is why they help it wet greasy cloth. Surface tension is a force per unit length acting in the surface. A soap bubble has two surfaces, so its excess pressure is 4S/r against 2S/r for a drop.
